Anker Soundcore P30i buds.
First and foremost I want to be clear that I am rating these buds purely on their own merit.  Without their software, without any Equalizer, just on how they perform straight out of the box.
Baseus and Tozo and Jlabs are some of the names when we think of Budget Bass Buds.  And for those who are looking for good, clean bass... I'd compare these with Jlabs.  For bass, right out of the box, playing music with bass in it, they deliver a clear, audible thump, without the actual pounding vibration.  Right now, I'm listening to Cry Little Sister, from the Lost Boys soundtrack, at volume EIGHT.  (That's not even halfway up my volume bar from my phone).
And the base tune soundstage is really, really good.  Especially for a bass tuned base.  The vocals, and background vocals are right up front.  Crisp, clear, and don't sound like they are being overwhelmed by anything.  And I can definitely hear every hit from the bass drums, as well as count the cords on the keyboard.
Now I'm at 12, and those bass drums are starting to pound.  Other than it's significantly louder, I'm still hearing good clarity of the different ranges.  I can't say this for my Tozo T18 Crystal buds, without tuning.
My Baseus BP1 pros would be creeping over the midrange at this volume on the base tune.
Ok, now I'm at 18.  A lot louder than I usually listen to.  The highs are much more prominent over the lows.  Which is the opposite of how a lot of bass speakers work.
Honestly, this kind of division of the ranges from a single driver speaker is kind of surprising, especially at 20 to 25 dollars.
Battery life is good too.  I have a 10 hour day.  2 hours on the bus, 8 hour shift at work.  With the ANC turned on, they need a quick charge at lunch to carry me home.  With ANC turned off, yeah, I can get back in the door before they need to be charged.  Sometimes just barely, if I've had them cranked up.
ANC- on the bus they do pretty good.  Cuts down a lot of the engine and sound noise from the bus.  I can still hear people talking next to me, but at about half what it would be without the buds in.
At work?  Well it's so noisy at work even full blown ear muffs aren't making it good.
Feel- ok this is subjective, because my right ear canal is different from my left.  In my right, I can feel a bit of pressure when I put them in.  But once in, they're quite comfortable, and I can fall asleep with them in, as a side-sleeper.
Bluetooth is good.  Stays connected as long as I'm in range, and range is definitely acceptable.  Definitely better than the chap 17 dollar Onn buds I have.  Easy to pair also.
My only real complaint is no front panel to show the charge on the batteries.
All said the bass isn't as deep on the base soundstage as Tozo delivers, but it's cleaner.  Tozo also offers much better options in their software, as does Baseus, in some ways.
I DO like a lot that SoundCore went the route of making the stems wider, instead of longer.  Having long hair, it's less likely to get caught on the stems, and pull them out.

Just got this and set it up ... have only used it for a day or two, but already can say it seems to be what I was looking for.
My computer setup and work is super ergo, with multiple monitors (at eye height!), orthonormal split keyboard, and everything adjusted as well as it can be.  BUT long days at the computer continue to take their toll, and in addition back and shoulder pain, I was starting to get hip and low back pain, presumably for all the slouching and poor postures than standard chairs tend to exacerbate.
I decide on this particular kneeling chair, because it is ADJUSTABLE.  This chair adjusts perfectly for me in the current setup, but I seriously doubt a general, "out of the box" (non-adjustable) configuration would have worked for this chair.
(Most office chairs are adjustable, body types just vary to much for one size fits all.  Kneeling chairs need to adjust, too!)
The chair is nice, solid and easy to put together.  They even sent a notebook and pen, and cute wooden phone holder.  Clearly, they care about their product and its purpose.
The chair still takes some getting used to.  With the correct adjustments, the height is actually a little more than I was expecting (for the height of my desk), but no problem, I got taller wrist wrests and raised my center monitor, and the whole setup is quite comfortable.
The most notable point is that it is really difficult to have bad posture in this chair.  It "forces" you to be upright, and also keeps you from slouching side-to-side, without feeling unnatural.  It's likely that I'll switch back-and-forth to the regular chair after some hours, in the same way that people with standing desks also sit periodically, or how there really is no one "most comfortable" position to sleep in - it's natural to change positions after some time.
The one odd thing is that there is really not much position for your feet.  This seems obvious, but I can't really put my feet flat, so they are pointed slightly (as they would be if you were sitting on your knees).  This is probably somewhat intrinsic to sitting chair, and is just ... part of the positioning.  It does also work to put one (or two) feet in front, on slightly cross the legs, for some variation while sitting.
But the general feel is just comfort, as I can tell my arms are actually hanging correctly (relief!), and there is just no stress or twist in my low back.  It does take a little effort, which is why I'll likely need to switch back to my standard chair periodically, but the effort is just a reminder, and easy way, to continually work on your posture.  I'm curious if this feel ever more comfortable, after a month of the mild stretching and strengthening that results from setting in this chair.
Overall, 100% happy with the purchase, and would recommend, especially to anyone who needs some additional ergo in their office setup.

- I am learning Spanish to be with orphan kids in Colombia.  I go to a church to be around them.  I have an S24 Ultra that can translate to text or voice.  I was wondering if it would be worth getting the S26 Ultra before going to Colombia again.  Battery life was the same and the processor was a lot faster.
- I expected go for it, but that's not the advice I received.  Instead I received your S24 Ultra already has the Galaxy AI Interpreter for face-to-face conversations, Live Translate for phone calls, excellent microphones, and plenty of AI processing power.  Samsung's newer hardware improves AI performance, but translation quality is mostly limited by speech recognition (understanding the speaker), translation model quality, context understanding, accents, slang, and background noise, not raw phone speed.  Going S24 Ultra to the S26 Ultra might get slightly faster response, smoother offline AI, maybe less delay, but it will not suddenly make Spanish conversation feel like a Star Trek universal translator.  Your S24 Ultra is already a monster.  For translation, the bottleneck is not your Snapdragon processor, it is capturing clean speech and the AI model doing the interpretation.  A better microphone path can help more than a faster phone.  The Samsung earbuds Buds4 Pro is what I would recommend.  The reason they matter is not that they magically translate by themselves, they improve the whole workflow.  The microphones are closer to your mouth, they reduce background noise, you can hear translations privately, and you are not always holding a phone between two people.  For example, with Galaxy AI Interpreter, you wear earbuds, the other person talks toward the phone, you hear English translation in your ear, your phone can output your voice translated Spanish.  Moreover, if you have a Samsung phone, Galaxy Buds can do some translation tricks too.
- It took me some time to overcome feeling stupid for spending 10x as much for something I had that works well, it was unimaginable that they could be that much better, and something I had to guard with my life now.  I ordered, then struggled with cancelling, and then let it go on the basis that I also wouldn't know unless I "rolled the dice" to know, and the importance of the mission.  The struggle was not the money.  It was feeling stupid after I already had some that worked fine.
Experience:
- Setup surprise:  Like all earbuds, they come with various sizes to fit your ears.  Unlike the others I have, it has a setup that tests and determines the size that fits your ear.  You do not do the determine which size, it does.  You get a green check when you get a size that passes.  There was only one of the sizes that passed, and they were not the same size for each ear.  When I had someone look at my ears and size of the opening, they said they are exactly the same.  I tried to trick it by changing its position to have it use the same size for each ear, but it wasn't buying it.  I'm guessing it detects how much escapes from the ear to the microphone.  Next it wants to do a hearing test like the flight surgeons used to do.  This takes a while.  Flight surgeons check to see if your hearing is still good.  This uses the results of the tests to profile your hearing sensitivity across frequencies to adjust the volumes to make it perfect for each ear.  That's more than my ~$1600 flight helmet does.
- Comparison:  My cheap ones worked just fine, I don't listen to music, and adjusting a mixer to the way I want to hear music just isn't a "duck in my pond".  I just want to hear the unaltered sound, clearly, and be understood clearly, that's all I care about.  You will not be able to imagine there could be a difference beyond that UNTIL you experience them side-by-side.  Then they are very different.  According to the scientific tests, the battle is between these and the ones from Apple, which are about the same price.  However, if you have a Samsung Phone, it's no contest, which I do, because the iPhone doesn't have the smarts , flexibility, ability to document and record my phone calls automatically, enable you to write scripts to automate things without external approval, or have both eSIM and nanoSIM, as often nanoSIM plans are much cheaper abroad for some reason unknown to me.  E.G. The iPhone is a great phone too, but it simply "cannot get there from here".
- Features:  It has different modes available to control the cancelling of background noise, one of which is to turn off the cancelling when you start talking so you can hear the response of the person next to you without removing the ear buds.  There is a mode for driving to hear alert noises.  It is much nicer for translation as mentioned in the advice I was given.  Like the AirPods, these are also water resistant.  You can also track and find them over the Internet from last place used, in Bluetooth range, and you can also find them in the case and turned off locally.  There is no tendency for them to fall out of my ears while running.
Summary:  These are a different ball game than the inexpensive ones.  If you have a use case like mine it is, and might also be worthwhile for someone whose hearing isn't the best.  What I've written should help you determine if the extra initial cost and cost if you lose them, is worth the advantages they bring for your use case.

I have owned a galaxy s24 since the end of 2024 and it is hands down the best phone I've ever owned, and because these are Samsung galaxy ear buds obviously they paired right up to them like they came with them. It even added a settings tab at the very top of my settings bar for quick access to all the ear bud settings which is awesome! I do like the pinch button as opposed to only having a touch button. It's easy to click and has a satisfying sound when you click it. They come with 3 size of rubber fittings for your ears and also have a "test fit" feature where they sense how well your ear bud fit. I use the ones that came on them because the were the best fit for my ears. I have to say that these are the most comfortable and lightest ear buds I've ever owned. This morning and i swear I'm not exaggerating, i almost panicked because i didn't feel the right one in my ear and thought i set it down so i started looking before i felt me ear with my hand and it was in my ear. I didn't feel it at all! And i use the ambient sound mode so i can hear everything with them in just as well as without them. When you first put them in and turn on ambient sound, you notice the sound as coming thru a speaker, but within 10 minutes of wearing them you get used to it or something because the sound becomes seamless and natural. When listening to music the sound is next level clear and crisp. With the noise cancelation on I'm able to wear them at work where im rebuilding swimming pool motors, so we use grinders and loud power tools daily and the general noise of working in a shop, and can still hear every word to the music and every note. They can't drown out that much background noise to where i don't hear the tools and i don't think any headphones out there would be able to pull that off, but for being little light earbuds they definitely cancel out most of the noise and enough to stop hear my music and notifications. I have not "exercised" with them in so i can't tell you about that, but i can't imagine they would be anything but awesome for working out considering how light weight they are and how secure they fit into the ear canal. I did read a few comments complaining about the battery life, but i have to say i think they hold a change for a decently long time. I wear them for my entire 10 hour shift at work, listening to music for about 3 or 4 hours of that if not more, and i haven't even seen a battery low warning yet.  And the case i just plug in every night like i do my phone and i never have a battery life issue, not yet at least. The 360 sound mode is really neat as well and i did try the directional sensor thing where it makes the sound seem like it is coming from the direction the video is, so as you turn your head the sound seems to be coming from the same direction as the screen and it's really neat but i don't keep it on because it's just... different. The only thing i have not tried is the live a.i. translation, but i will try that out next time i work my other job because we have plenty of Spanish speaking employees i can test it out with. So in conclusion, do i feel like these were a "well spent $280"? Only time will tell...
I'll update after six months if i haven't lost one by then.

Better fit for me than the Buds 2 and great sound cancelling.
Here's are my pros and cons:
Pro:
Comfortable for me and stays in my ear better than the Buds 2 and Buds 3. It doesn't feel like it's always on the verge of falling out, or that is plugging up my ear causing pressure in my ear.
Pro:
The case has a pairing button to make it easier to pair with your laptop and other non-phone devices.
Con:
When I had 2 devices paired with the Buds 4, it kept losing the connection to my laptop in the middle of use. I suspect there's a software bug.
Con:

Overall, the battery life and sound quality are good. At least as good as other ear buds that I've used over the past 15 years, and the stems do give you some pinch (pause or assistant) and swipe (volume or tracks) controls, like recent Apple'earpods.
But here's the one really big negative that earned these 4 stars instead of 5. Live translate. It sucks. I would much prefer to link to Google translate or something else. The Samsung version just doesn't work consistently. I tried it with a fluent Spanish speaker in a quiet room and it missed words, stopped listening mid sentence and was completely unreliable. Do not buy these if you need that feature. These are not a Babble Fish.
I would also prefer that the digital assistant was user selectible. I don't want to use Bixby, ever!
Otherwise, for listening to music and audio books, having a phone call or Zoom meeting, these are great and comfortable for long periods of time.

Overall I'm very satisfied with the desk, but I can't give this five stars due to the misleading measurements. The advertised 28 inch depth is including the height adjustment console that sticks out on the right side, which makes the actual depth 27.5 inches. I only noticed this after assembling the desk as the mat I planned to use on it was, you guessed it, 0.5 inches off. It's not the end of the world, but now the end of my mat has to either rest on top of my monitor arm or jut out from the front.
My other complaints aren't really complaints but they're things to keep in mind before purchasing, as they're the natural compromises that I made before purchasing a desk this size at such cost effective price.
First, the desk is not as wobbly/shaky as I was expecting it to be. Which is to say for my use case there's a a very light shake with large mouse movements that I only notice when thinking about it. I only notice a wobble when my monitor on a cheaper arm mount is reacting to it, which is probably more to blame on the arm mount than the desk. The heavy duty arm mount is very stable. On a separate note, the desk is not the thickest so I would recommend reinforcement plates if you do choose to install monitor arms on it. So far it is sustaining two single arm mounts just fine, aside from aforementioned wobble on the cheaper arm.
Second, as this isn't a single board desk, there is a seam separating the two boards. For me this is covered up by two different desk pads (one hard, one thick) so it's a non-issue, but it isn't seamless and has a bit of an edge to it so do keep that in mind if you don't plan to cover it up in some way.
Third, the height adjustment console runs pretty warm (not hot) while in standby. I'm considering on leaving it unplugged once I'm content with the height I like due to this for some peace of mind, as I don't really need an on demand height adjustment for my current use case.
All in all I think this is a good budget stepping stone to test the waters before looking into the standing desk endgame of buying a premium standing desk frame and a large slab of wood to make your own desk, as it becomes a much more lucrative purchase once you start looking at desks better than this one in terms of price for the size/quality.

Every now and then I like to treat myself. I’m not a big spender but I do know what I like. I’ve been an OLED display fan for as long as I remember and my first OLED was a tablet, another Samsung product. To my eye , I’ve yet to see another display type that offers the same levels of color fidelity, black levels and sharpness.
I’m not a gamer so things like super-fast refresh rates are somewhat moot to me but I do work on a computer a lot and consume a lot of media in the form of movies and TV. My main display is an LG OLED but in my bedroom system (which also includes 5.1 audio) I was suffering with a 27” LCD TV doubling as a monitor. That was OK for office work and browsing but its gray like black levels were a distraction when watching content with the lights off.
The prices of OLED monitors were putting me off but when this model dropped under four hundred bucks I decided to go for it. I’m glad I did. I'm unfortunately not able to go with a larger size in the space I have available, otherwise I would probably have gone for a dual purpose 42" or 48" TV/OLED monitor a while back. This 27' size is, however perfect for my current needs.
It is an entry level model. The body is plastic, it has limited inputs: one HDMI and one Display Port. It does have a USB-A socket but that’s for service only; it won’t accept media files for display. The resolution is 1440p. I was a bit concerned at the lack of 4K but that proved not to be a problem. There are no speakers but you can pass-through audio via a 3.5 mm socket for headphones or computer speaker hookup.
I didn’t use the included stand, instead choosing to mount the screen on a cantilever arm for ease and flexibility.
When I first turned on the TV, connected to my computer over Display Port, the colors seemed overbright (this is common) and the color balance was way off. This was quickly cured by entering the “original” mode and matching the visuals with my LG laptop which this works in tandem with when I’m computing.
For AV consumption, I’m feeding the HDMI input with sources from a Roku Express 4K streamer and an Oppo BDP-93 Blu-ray player. At first I thought the visuals were a bit “meh!” but then I realized that my surround receiver, which these devices were routed via, topped out at 1080p resolution. When I connected the monitor directly to the Roku via HDMI, the Roku was fooled into thinking the Samsung was a 4K device and the monitor down-rezzed the signal to 1440p without issue. I have to say, the difference between 1080p upscaled and 4K downscaled was like night and day. Fed with a decent 4K HDR signal, I was hard pressed to tell any difference in quality between what I was seeing on this monitor and the picture on my much larger 4K LG OLED TV in the living room. The picture was superb. Of course that meant I had to ditch my older Marantz receiver and replace it with a more recent version with 4K capability in order to get the best out of the screen. The newer Marantz is also able to upscale my Blu-Ray discs from the OPPO and they look great on this device.
Now I couldn’t be happier. I can watch movies and TV in bed in the highest quality imaginable. Everything is super-sharp. Colors are still maybe a little overblown (especially in the blue thru’ teal area) but it’s not a dealbreaker. Skin tones, light reflection, space scenes; everything looks mind blowing.
The menu system is quite intuitive once you get used to it and I’m now capable of navigating around quite freely. That said, I have downloaded Samsung Display Manager to my computer to perform the most common tasks like input switching without using the main power/menu input button. I’ve heard this can be quite fragile and break easily and is often refused warranty coverage. Frankly, I’ll do anything to keep this going as long as possible. It’s perfect for my needs. Whether browsing web pages, typing documents, watching YouTube videos or consuming content from other devices, everything looks stunning on this. HDR works great despite a relatively low 200 nits average peak brightness level and black levels and shadow detail in the darkest areas are sublime.
This might not be the absolute best choice in OLED monitors (especially for avid gamers) but for most people, I don’t think they’d be missing the kind of specs that can cost hundreds of dollars more. This is a fine product at a very tempting price.

I was immediately interested in this adjustable weight system because it seemed like such a clever and compact way to store multiple dumbbell weights. I currently have 5-, 7-, 8-, 10-, and 15-pound weights scattered around my house, so the idea of replacing all of that with a single unit offering 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25 pounds was very appealing. Having everything consolidated into one compact system is ideal, especially when storage space is limited.
When I opened the box, the handle and weight plates were packaged separately from the plastic base. I actually appreciated that because shipping the entire unit assembled could have potentially resulted in a cracked base. Both pieces arrived in perfect condition.
The system comes with an instruction manual explaining how to set up and adjust the weights. I’ll be honest, though: either I’m missing something obvious, or the instructions could be much clearer! Once I figured it out, the mechanism itself was quite simple. There are small weight markings—5, 10, 15, and so on—on the center section of the handle. You rotate the handle to select the desired weight, then simply lift it from the base with the appropriate plates attached.
Returning the handle to the base can occasionally require a little wiggling and giggling—I mean *jiggling*—to get everything lined up properly and allow the unused plates to settle back into place. It’s not a major issue, but it does take a little getting used to.
One thing I really appreciated was the additional exercise guide. In addition to the manual, there is a separate sheet featuring dozens of exercises with pictures and descriptions. That’s a particularly nice touch for anyone who is new to strength training or simply wants some ideas for different exercises.
There are a couple of things worth knowing before purchasing. First, this is a single-weight system, so you can only work one arm at a time. This is clearly stated in the product description, so it wasn’t a surprise or disappointment for me. In fact, unilateral exercises can be beneficial because they require your core to work harder to stabilize your body.
The second issue is the feel of the handle at certain weight settings. When using 10 or 20 pounds, the weight feels nicely balanced because the plates are distributed more evenly. At 5, 15, or 25 pounds, however, the weight distribution is more uneven, making the handle feel somewhat cumbersome. It isn’t necessarily a deal-breaker, but it does take some getting used to.
Overall, I’m a happy camper with this system. The compact storage and convenience more than make up for the slightly unusual feel of the handle. My favorite part may actually be how easy it is to find when I want to work out. In the past, having dumbbells scattered around the house meant I sometimes had to hunt around for the right weights. By the time I found them, something else could easily distract me, and I’d unintentionally skip the workout altogether.
Now everything is in one place and ready to go, which removes one more excuse.
Of course, there’s one final thing worth remembering: simply owning adjustable weights isn’t going to make you stronger. You actually have to use them!

I am a professional software engineer and computer enthusiast. I have used no fewer than a half dozen mechanical keyboards as my daily driver over the past few years, from brands like Corsair, Asus ROG, Logitech, and Lofree. This one is by far and away the best keyboard I have ever tried.
I do not write product reviews very often, but it feels so good to type on this that I just wanted an excuse to use it more.
This is the only keyboard I have ever encountered that does not leave me wanting for more features. I use and develop software on both Mac and Windows PC machines, so having a built-in switch to toggle between these different platforms is a game changer. The option to connect it via 2.4GHz adapter, Bluetooth, and directly via USB-C cable makes it incredibly versatile. I really appreciate the Bluetooth connectivity in particular, as it is surprisingly low latency and makes it super easy to switch between up to three connected devices in roughly a second (which is very useful when working on multiple machines simultaneously).
The ability to fully customize the keyboard on the web is another huge perk. I have found that the Keychron launcher website is fairly intuitive and works well, and I am very pleased that I do not have to download another piece of software in order to get the most out of this keyboard. Though you can only configure the settings via the web interface when the keyboard is connected via USB-C cable, the settings get flashed to the board's internal persistent storage, so all of your settings (such as remapped keys and custom RGB profiles) still work when in Bluetooth or 2.4 GHz mode.
But maybe most importantly is that from a pure aesthetic and feel standpoint, it looks, feels, and sounds awesome. The RGB lighting is subtle enough to not be too distracting for a workplace but vivid enough to add a cool accent. It is also very usable with the RGB backlight turned off, as it is not needed for readability. And I cannot emphasize enough just how good the feel is. I would say that the magnetic switches on this board respond most comparable to linear (red) switches from other manufacturers (which are my personal favorite kind) but with slightly more resistance that makes accidentally triggering keys less frequent. I find that I genuinely make fewer typos on this board compared to some of the other products I have tried. Controlling the key actuation depth is a really cool bonus feature, but I honestly find the default setting to be perfect.
If I could find anything negative to say about this keyboard, it would be that the battery life is only ok. While some of the other keyboards I have tried have batteries that can last for more than a full work week of use, I find this one drains fairly quickly. It's enough to get me through about two day's worth of work before I have to plug it back in, but given that it is still fully usable in wired mode, I honestly don't find this to be too big of a deal. Otherwise, the list of cons pretty much ends there.
Simply put, for $140, this board is an incredible value. It takes a really special product for me to take the time and write out a review, but this board is just that good.

I’ve been using this chair for a bit now and it’s been a genuinely upgrade. The build quality stands out right away, it has real heft and doesn’t feel cheap or hollow. Everything fits together cleanly and once assembled it feels stable and planted. I’m over 6 ft and 200+ lbs and it handles that without any issue, no creaking or sense that it’s being pushed to its limits.
There’s enough space in the seat and back that you don’t feel boxed in. I added an extra ergonomic cushion and it still feels roomy, which isn’t always the case with chairs in this category. The adjustability helps a lot here, especially the lumbar support. Being able to move it up and down and also forward and back makes it easy to actually get it where you need it, instead of just accepting a fixed position. The armrests are also easy to dial in, especially if you’re switching between typing, reading, or leaning back a bit. The tilt range is useful, and the tilt tension is stronger than I expected. Even at my size it takes a bit of effort to lean back, which I see as a positive since it feels controlled and supportive rather than loose or overly easy to recline. The mesh is another strong point. It came in perfect condition, no snags, no loose threads, no rough edges anywhere. There weren’t any bits of untrimmed plastic on the frame either, which says a lot about the quality control. The mesh itself is taut with a bit of bounce, so it doesn’t sag but still has some give, which makes long sitting sessions more comfortable.
Assembly was straightforward and clearly thought through. The instructions are easy to follow, but what stood out were the built in redundancies that keep you from second guessing anything. There are multiple left and right indicators when installing the arms, a clear front facing marker for the gas lift, and the screws are labeled in the packaging so you’re not guessing which goes where. It’s one of the smoother assembly experiences I’ve had.
I also reached out to activate my warranty and had a very positive experience. I spoke with Alice who was very knowledgeable, quick, warm, and they went out of their way to help me with whatever I needed. When I inquired about the extra screw holes under the chair, she let me know that this was for a foot rest which was still in the production phase and unprompted offered to have one shipped to me when they were ready! I'd resisted the wireless headphone trend for as long as possible, preferring the regular 3.5mm jack. Unfortunately, iPhone thought it would be a good idea to get rid of the headphone jack altogether. I disagree with this decision, but I don't make phones, so... I used regular wired headphones with a connector thingy to be able to plug it into my phone for a while. That worked fine, except for the fact that the connectors would inevitably stop working after a while. So I went through many of those. Then one day, my phone stopped working with connectors. No matter what I did, the volume would go back to zero and I couldn't use the headphones at all. So finally I decided to get wireless headphones, even though I once heard it's like the equivalent of putting a microwave in each of your ears. Oh well, it's 2026 and wifi and 5G and whatever else is all over the place. But then I had to go down the rabbit hole of finding headphones that were worth it. I didn't want super expensive or fancy wireless headphones for listening to music with my phone. I have over-ear Sony headphones that I use for recording and sound editing, I just really needed something to listen to music on my phone with while going for a walk. Reading reviews was frustrating and took me all over the place. Finally I decided to go with my gut and just order these. They're fine. I'm a bit of a sound snob and I need bass. These are fine. They fit well enough and comfortable enough in my ears. They don't get as loud as I would prefer, but that's probably a good thing. The bass is decent. The overall sound feels balanced for the most part. They hold a charge for a long time, too. I've only charged the case once since I bought them a couple months ago and I don't even know if they were close to needing a charge. I only really use them when I go for a walk around the neighborhood. I use them to listen to music and have not tried to use them for a call or anything. They seem easy to use, though admittedly I don't care to be bothered to learn what all the various tap combinations do. I put them in my ears, they automatically pair with my phone after the initial pairing, and I use the controls on my phone for volume and track changes. This works for me. They are fine. I do not think ANY wireless headphones have the sound quality of wired headphones, so these are fine. The sound is fine. I'm not like, "oh wow! these are amazing!" but I am happily listening to tunes as the soundtrack to my walks. I like how they fit in the case and its easy enough to throw them in my purse. I almost dropped one once, and I did not like that feeling of not being able to catch them with a cord but, that's me. I will say it is nice not to have to deal with the cord in terms of it being in the way while walking around or getting tangled in a purse. I have no idea about the water resistance because that's not something I deal with while wearing headphones. In terms of noise cancellation... it's not something I've really noticed, but now that I think about it I don't really notice the sound of the traffic/cars on the street while I am walking. This may or may not be a good thing. But I am happy with them. For the price, I am happy with them. For the sound, I am happy with them. For the purpose of walking while listening to music, I am happy with them. If you are also going down the rabbit hole of reviews trying to find basic earbuds for music listening purposes, I do suggest getting these and saving yourself any more frustration. They're not perfect, they're not incredible, but they are just fine.

As for these ear buds, it may be helpful to consider what you expect to use them for and what your expectations are. My ears never have hurt or get “sore” after long use (more than 5 hours). I realize that this is subjective, but I have smaller ear holes and the ear tips are soft and associated supports that go around the driver fit my ear very well and provide lasting light comfort. These earbuds are not overly heavy at all.
I have an Apple iPhone, and have found connectivity to be very little problem at all. It connects without issue and plays all my apps very seamlessly, Spotify, YouTube, Audible phone calls all the rest no issues whatsoever. I have not tested water resistance in that sense however walking in the rain no issues, with sweat doesn’t seem to be any issue. I’m anal about keeping them clean and I would encourage you to do the same. They seem durable and not flimsy or cheap.
Finally, we get to the most important part for me at least and that is the quality of the sound coming through them for music. I am not an audiophile, at least not in the sense that I think about other sounds snobbery, but I do love my music and I know what it should sound like if you like the U curve or the typical rock curve you will love these earbuds. The base is rich, but not distorted, the mids are very good, and the highest trebles are not hissy, but crisp. Equalizer in the app only has three settings, but I still think it’s useful and helpful. However, you’ll have to use other settings if you have an iPhone to get it dialed in to your liking. Fortunately, I was able to do that to get better volume and better control in concert with Apple iPhone settings turning off Spotify equalizer and sticking to the Bose app for controlling the quality of the sound and it did work well. iPhone has a setting in which it limits the volume, adjust that setting and your volume will increase by I would say 20% maybe a little more, I have them dialed in now. And having them dialed in I think the sound is excellent and very enjoyable. I think these are well worth the purchase and have enjoyed them for the time. I’ve owned them with no issues with charging or any other issues. Highly recommended. Give them 5 stars.

I have owned the Samsung Galaxy Buds Plus, Jabra Elite 85t, and Bose Headphones 700, and I currently use the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (2nd Gen).
Fit and Comfort: The Bose are very comfortable and stay securely in my ear, unlike the Samsung Galaxy Buds Plus. A poor fit was the main reason I moved on from the Samsung—they simply wouldn't stay in.
Sound Quality: The sound on the Bose is excellent. It is significantly better than my old Jabra earbuds and even surpasses my Samsung Galaxy Buds Plus, which I already thought were quite good.
Noise Cancellation: The noise canceling is hands-down the best I’ve experienced. It easily beats the Jabra 85t, which had mediocre noise canceling at best, and it's superior to the Samsung Galaxy Buds Plus. For example, I was recently at a noisy Chicago O'Hare terminal on a call; the person I was talking to had no idea I was in a loud airport because they couldn't hear any background noise. Additionally, as a frequent flyer, I find they do a great job filtering out jet engine noise, even on a 10-hour international flight.
Connectivity Issues: The 'Connect-to-Talk' speed is terrible. While the Samsung and Jabra buds connected almost instantly when removed from the case, the Bose are very slow. Often, a call will go to voicemail before the Bose connect, or I have to wait several seconds for the sound to kick in after answering. This is incredibly frustrating.
Controls and App: The touch controls are poor; I still can't figure out the timing or pressure required, and I constantly trigger them accidentally just by adjusting the fit. The software app also feels like an afterthought. It frequently fails to recognize the earbuds even when they are actively connected via Bluetooth to my S25+ or tablet. I often have to reinstall the earbuds in the app just to get it to see them. I don’t have these issues with my Bose 700 headphones or my previous Jabra and Samsung apps.
Verdict: While the sound and ANC are world-class, the slow connectivity, poor app, and finicky touch controls are bad enough that I am looking for other solutions. I’m hoping the Samsung Buds 4 Pro can match this noise reduction while providing a more reliable app and faster connection speeds.

This led to poor ANC and sound quality issues. I love having swipe controls for volume as I use them often, and having control parity between buds was important to me. -swipe controls (this is subjective)
-sound quality (it sounds just so much wider and bigger than other buds I've used)
-android compatibility (when I open the case, it shows the battery level of the case and each bud in my notifications)
-Mic sounds pretty good even in wind so far
-ANC performance is stellar. I can barely hear plates clanging together at my gym now. They also don't plug my ears up badly like some other ANC implementations can do.
-No foam eartips (subjective, but I find them unbearable. The included tips also have a wax barrier)
-No issues with the battery life so far, looking forward to testing more on my next intl. flight.
Cons:
-Some initial comfort issues with the wingtips, but this subsides after a few days of wear
-While the case is wireless charging compatible, I find it super hard to get it to trigger on most pads
-The buds orientation in the case is a bit odd and makes it hard to get the buds out unless you pluck them a certain way. Not a huge deal, but worth mentioning considering the price.
-The app isn't the most intuitive
Overall, no regrets on this purchase, especially when they're on sale.

I purchased two of these 34 inch 4K curved  monitors to use in my home office environment.  I have multiple windows open at the same time, and using a single 42" monitor still didn't give me the flexibility I wanted, hence two of these.
They arrived yesterday and firstly, I have recently purchased monitors online only to have them arrive with a cracked screen. These are very well packaged and were perfect out of the box. That said, assembly of the simple but effective stand was three screws and all done.  Very stable on my work surface.  I am using a Windows 11 Pro laptop that has all the bells and whistles, and connect external devices through a hub / port.  Now, here is why my review has the headline as you see it.
After hooking everything up (power and HDMI and you're done), and booting my computer, I had one display that was gorgeous with 4K resolution, and the other so blurry I couldn't read it at 640x480 resolution.  ??  It goes without saying that all of my Bios, drivers, and connections were solid, cables were good, etc.  Windows would not let me select a resolution on the second monitor - it was all grayed out.  I tried the monitor setup button itself - no joy as the resolution is controlled by the computer graphics card.  I re-booted, I swapped cables, still no joy.  Obviously this is a simple user-error, but it was really late in the day and beyond me to figure it out.
I called the toll free number for Tech Support that was in the setup guide, and they have hours until early evening PST (I'm EST) so that was good.  And then - after going through the call directory for Tech Support I got the dreaded recording "All agents are assisting other customers.  You  may leave a message or try again later."  Yeah - right; we've all heard that before.  So, I left a message that I needed setup help, my name and number, and went downstairs to fix some dinner.
Here's the incredible part, and the First Shock.  Less than 15 minutes and my cell rings and it is Sceptre Tech Support!  Not a robot - a person!  I went back to my home office, and started by telling the very polite young man (who spoke impeccable English) that I had just unboxed these and had not even registered them yet.  Second Shock - he didn't put me through name, address, email, phone, model, serial number, and the rest of the gamut that is normal.  He simply asked what my problem was and what I had tried.  We walked through that, changed around one connection, re-booted, and all was perfect!  Third Shock - he stayed with me through it all, made sure I could shut down and start up without difficulty or change in display quality, confirmed monitor settings for my usage profile, and then took some extra time to tell me about features I had seen in the user guide that might be beneficial for me given my use, and walked me through those as well.
I can promise you I will tell this story again and again.  Beyond that, I'm going to look at everything this company sells and - if I have a need - I will buy their products.  Those of you in the electronics world will understand how extraordinary this level of customer interaction is in today's world. I wish I had this person's name, as he deserves the accolades, but he didn't give it - he just was there to help.
Wow . . .

The Sceptre 34-Inch Curved Ultrawide WQHD Monitor has been a fantastic addition to my setup, and after owning it for two years, I can confidently say it’s been reliable and well worth it.
The 3440 × 1440 ultrawide resolution looks fantastic and gives you a ton of screen real estate. Whether I’m multitasking, gaming, or just browsing, everything looks sharp. The R1500 curve also makes a noticeable difference—it pulls the edges of the screen into your field of view.
Build quality has held up well over time, and I’ve had no reliability issues after two years of regular use. For the price, the features you get—ultrawide WQHD, high refresh rate, and good color reproduction—make this monitor a strong value.
The only real downside is the power/menu button design. The button is located on the bottom of the monitor and acts as an all-in-one control for power, menu, and navigation. It works, but it can be a bit awkward and unintuitive to use, especially when you’re trying to quickly adjust settings.

• Owned for 2 years with no issues
• Sharp 3440 × 1440 ultrawide resolution
• Smooth 165–180Hz refresh rate
• 1ms response time
• Good color with 99% sRGB
• Excellent value for the price
Cons
• Single bottom button for power and menu navigation can be awkward
Overall, if you’re looking for an affordable ultrawide monitor with great performance and reliability, this Sceptre model is a solid choice. After two years of use, it’s still performing exactly as expected.

I have tested numerous “smart watches” in my quest to find a decent replacement for my ever faithful and reliable, Fitbit Versa 4. I purchased it almost four years ago to replace the original Fitbit Versa. But then Google took over Fitbit, and I was looking for a reliable alternative to the Fitbit products. I tried a Samsung Galaxy watch 7 that lost steps by the thousands each day. I tried an Apple Smart Watch that sometimes had to be charged more than once EVERY DAY! I tried a Parsonver (less expensive) but even though it was advertised and labeled IP 68, (indicating that it would withstand submersion in water) I actually received an email from the company before the watch was even delivered advising me to be careful even showering or washing my hands with it on! SERIOUSLY???? And the step counts were not even close to correct!  Then I tried an Amazfit BIP6 (also advertised as IP 68, but clearly IS NOT) and thought I had finally found what I was looking for, until it completely malfunctioned after only 3 weeks of use. So Amazon replaced it with ANOTHER BIP6, and that one lasted almost 5 months before it began to seriously malfunction and the touchscreen no longer worked. So my new search began and I decided to give Garmin a try as my walking and swimming buddies swear by their Garmins, and the results that they get with them compare favorably to my old Fitbit. I have now only had the Garmin Vivoactive 5 for about a month, but so far, it is AWESOME! It tracks extremely well with the Fitbit, and I have had no issues whatsoever with water infiltration. If that changes, I will be back to downgrade my rating, but so far, so GREAT! This proves that you don’t have to buy the most expensive models of ANY brand of fitness watch to find one that does what you need it to do. Most of them have more functions than you will ever need or use anyway. I bought separate, different color bands to customize it and love that you have a lot of choices for watch faces, so pick the one that works best for you! (Although - once again, Fitbit has a much better and more user friendly watch face selection portal!)
The one potential “glitch” I thought I had finally discovered with my Vivoactive 5, but which turned out not to be an issue, occurred when I was flying internationally. I was returning from Europe to the US on an evening flight where the time in the US was six hours earlier. So both my FITBIT and my Garmin thought that when enough flight time had elapsed, they went past midnight and started their metrics over as a new day - meaning steps completely zeroed out and started over. But not long after I landed at 7 pm US time, my Fitbit picked back up with the previous day’s step tally, but my Garmin still showed the reduced step count tallied as a “new day”. I was disappointed with this until I checked the metrics in the Garmin app and noted that the “two day tallies” indicated on the watch itself were actually (appropriately!) counted and displayed as a single day step counts in the app. So yes, I am sold on the Garmin. But I do still have to wonder why if FITBIT - even early versions - could have successfully addressed ALL of the issues I have found with so many competitor brands, why can’t all the others? Maybe I shouldn’t have been so wary of Google taking over Fitbit when I started investigating other Smart watches, but I learned a lot about different brands and their bogus IP 68 and 5 ATM ratings!
So to reiterate, Garmin is exactly what it says it is, and Fitbit is as well. Do your comparisons!

I'm coming from an Apple Watch Series 5. I had gotten frustrated with the battery life and sleep tracking and wanted to see if a more fitness-focused watch would be a better fit. I'm not a big runner or someone who does a lot of intense exercise, but I do like to track my exercise and sleep and get nudges to move when I've been sitting down for too long. I also like to get notifications on my wrist without needing to pull out my phone.
Compared to the Apple Watch, the first major thing I noticed was this is nowhere close in terms of smarts. I had gotten used to Apple's smooth interface, built in microphone and speaker for voice commands, and often useful apps that can be used without needing to get my phone out. That being said, after a few days I can confidently say that I don't need them. I would argue that Garmin knows what this is and what it is not - it's a fitness device first and foremost, and everything else comes second. And on that basis they nailed it - the fitness tracking has been excellent and noticeably better than the Apple Watch especially in sleep tracking. I also much prefer their approach to goals, which tracks exercise over the course of a week rather than focusing specifically on individual days. Whenever I was sick or had a down day I would feel guilty if I didn't close all of my rings on my Apple Watch, but I don't feel that same pressure with the Garmin. I do miss being able to use voice commands with my watch, but I could have gotten a more expensive Garmin if I really wanted that, and I don't think it's worth it for me.
The second thing I noticed: not having to charge your watch every day is a game changer. This was easily my biggest frustration with the Apple Watch since it's marketed as a device you wear 24x7 and yet needs to be charged every day. And considering how long it took to charge my Series 5, this was a major annoyance. I couldn't charge it overnight, because I wanted sleep tracking. I couldn't charge it in the morning, because I like to start off my day with exercise and it doesn't charge fast enough to do it after a workout and before work. And if I charged it in the evening, I would often forget to put it on before bed and miss out on the sleep tracking. The Garmin is a breath of fresh air by comparison - I charge it about once a week, and with my relatively light usage it can probably go close to two. I took a multi day trip recently and I didn't once have to worry about charging my watch, which was a pleasant change.
Overall I think this watch is a great fit for a more casual user who isn't running marathons but wants to track fitness and sleep and get some extras like smartphone notifications and see the weather at a glance. If you want something with more smart features and better build quality (i.e. more metal and less plastic), then the Venu might be a better fit. Or they have the Forerunner if you do run marathons. Or a bunch of other models for more specific use cases. But I would highly recommend giving this watch a try if you're looking for the same things that I am.

But for those not running with the gps every day or constantly tinkering with it a full battery charge seems to last a week. That is, charge it for an hour on Sunday and no need to charge it again until the same time next Sunday. You could get the battery to last longer if you’re willing to shut off absolutely everything that might use more power.
I started out with a Garmin vivosmart 5 because I didn’t think I needed anything beyond that, but I have sleep problems and decided I needed better sleep tracking. So I ended up with this one even though I don’t really care about random silly “apps” on a watch.
Overall this watch has been excellent. It has a very good UI and the fitness tracking features a quite good. The sleep tracking is decent, but still has its issues that hopefully Garmin will fix with software updates. In particular the “nap tracking” doesn’t seem fully baked yet, and things like laying back in a recliner reading a book or watching TV can get falsely detected as a “nap”. Then there’s no way to delete a false nap on the watch or in the Garmin Connect app.
There are still a few minor bugs that some people will run into but they seem to be things that can be fixed with firmware updates and I haven’t run into anything completely feature-breaking.
If you feel like messing with it you can also install some “apps” like custom watch face designs or sunset/sunrise times, more detailed weather and such. But even without installing anything the watch does everything needed for health and fitness stuff.
Almost all of the apps that come with the device can be uninstalled, so if you don’t need “women’s health tracking” for example then you can just remove that to free up space.
Their mobile app is pretty well designed and only awkward in some parts of the configuration.
The watch reliably synchronizes as long as you leave the phone app running in the background and I’ve never had any Bluetooth connection failures, lag, or lost pairings.
Things that the watch is not good for are things that you’d typically use a phone for like communication, turn by turn navigation, maps, games, and such. But I don’t want a watch to do any of that stuff and I’d rather have it save its battery charge so I don’t have to charge it constantly.
So overall, this is “the” watch you want if you want as little nonsense as possible and don’t want to worry about battery charge all the time but still need full health and fitness tracking stuff beyond what the $75-150 models offer. And there are also no subscriptions required.

I got the E25's, black. Packaging is nice, comes with a brief, clearly written user manual which I used right away to see how to change the sound options. I use a Samsung Galaxy S20 FE 5G, and I took these buds out of the package, directly out of the case and put them right in. The default female voice told me they were powered on right away, sounding in both ears, in the order i put them in. Opened bluetooth options on my phone and they were already listed as "Raycon Everyday Buds." I touched the name and they connected right off without any issue whatsoever. Hit play on my music, and I love the sound. I just opened them today, so I'm waiting to see how these endure before giving full stars.
The button in each bud is a physical push button, a bubble that clicks. I like it because the sweaty strap from my bike helmet won't press it inadvertently like my old buds that just had "touch control." You can't see the bud when you reach up to touch it, so it's always a game of fumbling with where to touch it and how many "touches" would register. Especially when on the mountain bike, that frustrated me, but maybe you like it (wierdo)...
Sound quality:
I love all three modes. "Balanced, Bass and Pure" they all sound good while bringing in their individual strengths. For piano pieces, like Paul Cardall or Ludivico Eiunadi, Pure Sound is precise. For Van Halen, Nightwish, and Godsmack, Balanced sound and Bass modes are excellent. It's all subjective anyway, but I can hear the details and fairly crisp sounds.
Awareness Mode:
This is my first time trying buds that have a mode where they claim to allow you to hear ambient noise around you while still enjoying the music. Raycon calls it "Awareness Mode". It works, but not as i had hoped. In my mind, I had anticipated being able to speak while listening to my music and hear my voice and others' clearly through the electronic mic instead of through jawbone vibrations like when you plug your ears with your fingers and speak. These buds can do that, but you can only hear it faintly, and I find myself wishing I could turn up that volume. But if I turn it up, only the music gets louder and the ambient sounds are left behind as the music grows in volume. The ambient sound volume is constant, and only works well if I turn the music off. Which is a disapponting feature because then what's the point? Without the music, I might as well remove the buds right? All buds claim to have powerful noise canceling, but what I'm hoping for is exactly the opposite, I want to hear my music and all the ambient sounds while biking, running, and working at my computer. It should be like hearing the world around me but with cool music that nobody else can hear. Why isn't this an option? Maybe I'm the wierdo.
The fit is okay... It comes with multiple gel sizes. The default sizes were a bit tight, so I downsized them by one, and they are comfortable for about 15 minutes then I have to push them in again. Not quite settled on which size of gel I should be using. This shouldn't be that difficult but...
UPDATE: 8/24/22
I've had them for over a month now. Still working as they did they day I opened them.
*The container charges in just a couple hours
*The longest I have had these in is about 5 hours, my ears became fatigued from the fit before the battery ran out while I was backpacking. The buds charged up and container still had more than 50%
*PHONE CALLS: I haven't had problems hearing clear audio from the phone calls. When I ask the other caller how I sound they have told me I'm difficult to hear well. If i turn off Bluetooth and speak directly into the phone they report my sound as being much better. Not impressed with the microphone quality. But I have had no problems at all hearing the other caller clearly.
*I have not yet had any connection problems with my phone
*I still am disappointed with the Awareness Mode.  It's very underwhelming compared to my daughter's Jabra Elite Active 75 earbuds with the same feature. Those are significantly better in this regard.
*I wear these while mountain biking, they stay in fine, but I don't bomb down the mountain either.
*I really wish I had the ability to adjust the equalizer settings but it's fixed in stone. The app is a complete joke, no functionality at all. No my friend, if you want to adjust the equalizer, these are not for you. I do wish I could adjust the bass to be more pronounced, and the highs to be a bit sharper.
12/2/2022 UPDATE: over 1 year ownership..
I still have these and they still work as described above, they hold charge forever. But at this point I'm ready for a different pair just because of the phone call quality and the weak awareness mode. I've also found that I can't remember how to use all the features because the push button functions aren't very intuitive, and no app to use for adjustments. I can answer a phone call, one push in either ear, but the quality is still reported as "difficult to hear." I'm going to be buying a different brand.
You should buy these if:
-You don't care about the awareness Mode
-You just want something that holds charge very well and will last a long time.
-Plays music with clear quality and have no desire to mess with sound settings.
-You want something with rock solid, reliable, connectivity.
You should not buy these if:
-You want to talk on the phone a lot

Yes, my subject line sounds like that trash hyperbole you get on annoying pop-up ads on your Smartphone! And ironically, it usually has to do with ear buds. There are tons of them on the market, and everyone claims to be the best.
Now, first off, I am just a customer… never got any gifts or money or anything from this company, nor was asked to “click on a review” for a discount or whatever. No… the reason for all this hallelujah chorus, is that I’m really totally both jazzed, and a bit in awe of these earbuds. I think the main mind-blowing thing about them is the price. I mean, I have a bit of experience and knowledge with this kind of technology, and frankly, these days, what “guts” that are needed to be used to create Bluetooth ear buds is not that complex… nor expensive. How company’s like Sony, Apple, Bose, etc. can charge upwards of $300 for these boarders on theft and fraud!
I’ve tried those “Rolls Royce” buds, and I urge you to do the same, and then try these Tagry Bluetooth Wireless Earbuds that are literally 90% less expensive. Yes, they retail for about $35! They come in an excellent quality charge base, are extremely easy to put on, (and have three extra size buds to give you a custom fit), and most important, their sound quality, and I mean crisp highs, solid middles, and bone- rumbling base, are outstanding. I cannot understand what more you would want either using them for talk radio, podcasts, YouTube, streaming movies, or TV, or playing your Amazon Music or Spotify or iTunes playlists. And yes, if connected to your iPhone, you can make and receive calls, and the microphone in the buds are top quality.
Their Bluetooth software is flawless, connecting to your iPhone, or other Bluetooth devices effortlessly. They come with a pleasant woman’s voice letting you know various messages, like which earbud is in what ear, if they are connected or turned off, your volume control (including excess volume warning), etc.
I’ve had these for several months, and have found the charging, which has a bright LED display and shows the individual charging of each bud, along with their percentage easy to read.
And a note on their service. I’ve heard horror stories of folks trying to reach the outrageously over-priced other earbud company’s for tech support, or refunds, exchanges, etc. Basically it’s nonexistent, and when you do miraculously find a phone number to call them, and get someone on the line, you have to go to the UN to find an interpreter of rare third-world languages to understand what they are saying, and they seem to be trained, not on anything to do with the product, but to make the call as useless and confusing as possible, so that you will just give up and throw their buds, and your money in the trash.
Now, I did have an initial problem, after a few months, in that the base charger seemed to be slowing a bit. Tagry gives you a LIFETIME WARRANTY… yes, an actually lifetime warranty, not one of those sham “lifetime warranties”, that corrupt company’s like Hammacher Schlemmer have.
I had enrolled with Tagry, on their website, to activate my warranty as soon as I received the buds. I called Tagry when I was seeing what could be a glitch in their charging base, and yes, unlike most other companies who hide their contact numbers as if they were nuclear codes, Tagry’s support phone number is plainly printed on their manual, and to my astonishment, I immediately was connected to a good ‘ol American customer service person, who actually worked for the company, spoke English, and made me feel as if I was a long-ago trusted friend. They truly cared, and said they were sorry, and that there was no need to troubleshoot the base, or return it, instead, they would process an order to send me a new one.
A day later, they actually called me back to let me know that the replacement had been shipped, and that I should have it in a day or so, and if not, to please call them back right away. And yes, to apologize again for any inconvenience. The replacement arrived the very next day. And again, their warranty is indeed for a lifetime, a no questions asked replacement policy. This is how much they believe in their product, and respect their customers.
So, yes. It is insane to pay more than $35 for quality Bluetooth earbuds. Last year, I sent about a dozen of these out to friends and employees, to use for personal use, and for all that Zooming going on… and they love them. And none of had any problems.
I’m sure you have had a plethora of bad experiences in the past few years, what with isolation, and way too much ordering on-line, finding the products you buy to be substandard, and customer service virtually non-existent. And that is why I’ve spend all this time expounding on the greatest of my earbuds. Yes, I have a life. Really. But what a joy to be able to tell a story like this, rather than the kind of frustration most of us are experiencing every day!
Yes, goodness and quality still exist. It’s rare… but it’s out there!

This review is about the audio features of the JBL Vibe Beam earbuds.
I'm an audio engineer so audio quality is very important to me. As such, I use wired connections as much as possible to maintain the integrity of the audio signal.  However, many newer consumer-level products no longer have audio jacks, so I finally decided to invest in some wireless earbuds as a backup to the other earphones and headphones that I use.  I didn't want to spend a lot of money as I didn't foresee myself using this product very much, and since this is my first foray into wireless audio earphones, if they were just ok or they broke after a while, then I wouldn't feel too bad about the little money that I spent.  Also, I wanted to focus on finding wireless earbuds with excellent audio quality first as I already have an excellent high-end bluetooth earpiece for cell phone use, and I wouldn't be using this product as a bluetooth headset for my phone.
After doing much research, I chose the JBL Vibe Beam's as they were at my price point, I'm familiar with JBL products, and I could reasonably expect that they were likely deliver the high audio quality that I've come to expect from JBL products.  In my research, I read reviews that complained about the harshness of the high end with high frequency instruments like cymbals or the lack of bass, so I was a bit concerned.
When I received and started listening to my JBL Vibe Beams I understood what people were talking about.  However, to correct the issues, first, one must have a great fit of the earbuds in their ears.  I'm fortunate, in that with the medium tips that were already installed on the Vibe Beams, they made a snug fit in my ears right out of the box.  If you find that these earbuds do not fit well in your ears it might be worthwhile to invest in a separate set of variable sized earbud tips, or try tips from one of your other well-fitting earbuds, if you have them.  Once the earbuds were seated properly in my ear, that took care of the poor bass issue. (I have not worn them long-term so I can't speak to them falling out of my ear, as others have mentioned, but they seem to stay in pretty well.)
For the misaligned frequency response issue, fortunately, the JBL Headphone app that you can install on your cell phone includes a ten-band graphic equalizer that you can use to make adjustments to the frequency response of your earbuds.  After listening to several of the reference tracks I use to check new audio equipment or my mixes against, I found that the only adjustments needed were carving out some of the upper midrange and making a very slight boost in the bottom end of the lower frequency spectrum.  I've included a screenshot of my EQ curve which I based on the Bass preset in the JBL app.  You can't tell as there is no dB scale on the side, but I needed to cut or boost by only 1-2 dB.  I find that my new EQ curve gives a more balanced frequency response than what came out of the box, and matches up well against the reference speaker system and headphones that I use for my audio mixing and mastering work.  I invite you to use my EQ curve as a starting point and adjust as sounds best to you.
I also read reviews complaining about the apparent lack of volume of the Vibe Beams.  I connected the JBL's to several different sources (phone, computer, TV, MP3 player, etc.) and I found that the overall maximum volume (with limiter off) is relatively lower than wired speaker versions.  However, the input to the JBL's is relative to the maximum output of the source itself.  I found that the loudest level I could get came from my iPhone and the lowest level output came from my MP3 player (which probably doesn't offer much output anyway being a tiny portable unit).  As a comparison, I did a side-by-side test of the JBL's with my wife's AirPods (2nd gen).  What I found was that the JBL's offered an almost identical audio output level as the AirPods with any of the sources I used so that confirmed that the output level of the JBL's has more to do with the source (and the source material as some songs are mastered at a lower volume than other songs) than with the earbuds themselves.  During my test, I put the JBL's at their maximum volume output (one tap at a time on the left bud to raise the volume).  Also, I noticed during my testing that the AirPods had a pleasing midrange sound perfect for listening to podcasts or watching video, but the JBL's excelled at full-range sound on the bottom and top ends of the frequency spectrum which made them sound much better over all and well-suited for music or listening to explosive action scenes in movies.
And speaking of movies, the JBL app has a switchable audio/video mode.  The video mode reduces the latency of the delivery of audio against picture, so there isn't a noticeable lip-sync issue with dialogue in a scene.  However, there is a slight degradation in the audio quality of 'video' mode versus 'audio' mode, but you will have to make the determination if the change in audio quality is acceptable to you.
As a side note, I included a picture of the inner side of the earbuds.  The 'L' and 'R' designations on the earbuds are tiny as you can see, plus they are the same color as the earbuds themselves, so they are very hard to see.  I wish JBL had made the L/R letters bigger or at least made them a different color so they would be easier to see.
The pairing process was fairly easy with all my bluetooth-capable devices and the range was good, only dropping out after walking approximately 60-70 feet from the source.  There was one momentary dropout during my listening but that could be due to my wife using her AirPods the same time as I was using the JBL's.
I can't speak to the other features of the JBL Vibe Beams as I don't intend to use them, but as far as audio quality goes, with just a few minor tweaks, these bluetooth earbuds can go from sounding like a $50 pair of earbuds to a $500 pair of reference earphones.

My husband and I had been wanting a glass air fryer for a while.  I'd been eying the Crispi, and when it went on sale we decided to get it, as we'd already been happy with the Ninja Foodi.  I saw when ordering that it came with 6 qt and 2.5 qt pans and the 4 qt one would need to be ordered separately.  Not a problem.
But it turns out it is also sold with the 6 and 4 qt pans with the 2.5 one to order separately, which would have been much better for us.  The smallest pan gets food too close to the element and we aren't really using it now that we bought the 4 qt pan.  So do check which options you're getting with your specific order.
The fryer itself is fantastic!  I've made wings, thick peppered bacon, asparagus, a whole chicken, sausages, and a ribeye steak.  My husband's done rolls and tater tots and turkey burgers.  The steak came out horrible (juicy enough, but this weird gold color, no Maillard reaction to speak of).  Could be a learning curve, could be the instructions I got were bad -- they certainly badly undercooked and underseasoned the steak, and I happen to like medium rare to rare, so this was -seriously- undercooked until I kept going.  However, everything else has been delicious.  And it's great to be able to eyeball the food as it goes, plus have the timer pause when you pull the pan out to flip the food.
Cleanup's a breeze.  The nonstick insert goes in the upper dishwasher rack, as does even the 6 qt pan.  I cut the worst of the grease out with detergent and rinse before dishwashing.  The only issue is that I can't tilt the pan in the rack and the rubber base has serious standing water in it after the cycle that needs blotting up with a paper towel, then some tilt time in the countertop drainer to get the liquid out that got trapped between base and glass.  People that are less averse than me to handwashing pots and pans might prefer to avoid the dishwasher.
The controls are also simple once you internalize that you must pick your setting before you press buttons for temp and time.
And, very happily, the countertop footprint is minimal if you have somewhere to put the glass pans.  They do stack with their lids on (note that the 6 qt pan has a bigger top, so don't mix up the lids; oddly all of them come with the same size nonstick insert, which doesn't seat as well in the smaller pans).  But I'm concerned about stacking more than two high, that's a lot of weight to press on a flexible rubber lid.

Can you give 10 stars? My 3 year old, $300+ dollar FitBit watch died after it got wet (must have gotten a crack somewhere). Anyway, as someone who exercises a lot I wanted another smart watch but this time hopefully a bit nicer looking than the old square FitBit Sense 2. I thought 'For $99 let's try it, I can return if I don't like it.'Ordered it at 10:00 pm the day my watch died, next morning at 7:00 it was here and I was wearing it by 7:30.
Just wow, wow, wow. So much better than my FitBit at 1/3rd the price. What I like better:
* 14 day battery life - that is legitimate - if you are just wearing (not tracking exercises, etc.) it will last at least 10 days, but usually about 2 weeks.
* When tracking an exercise activity - gives me more data, easier to read data, and overall does a better job than my fitbit
* Nicer looking - Round instead of square, lots of nice looking standard watch faces - in fact, it looks like a real watch with some of the faces
* Stays connected to my Google Pixel - My FitBit did this OK, but regularly it would disconnect from the phone and then you couldn't see weather, it wouldn't update data online to read, etc. This watch, I think it has disconnected maybe once since I purchased it
* Charged from 8% to 100% in just over an hour
* So many additional options around tracking sleep, taking breaks, tracking oxygen, etc.
* My FitBit said 'You got 4 hours of sleep' every day - even though I went to bed at 10:00 and got up at 6:00. I thought I must not sleep well. First night, this one capture 6.8 hours or something - seemed much more accurate
* Have not tried to actually make or receive calls on it, but it does let me know when my phone is receiving a call
* Can download and play podcasts and music from the watch
* Very accurate when tracking a route - I mountain bike, it is always within a half mile of what my bike says mileage ridden after a 15 mile ride
So, you can get a square FitBit that looks like a workout watch and spend $250. You can spend $500 or more for an Apple watch - and what if you are an Android user, Apple watch still works, but can't really connect well to my phone. Or, you can get one of these for $99, get as much and more functionality than a FitBit and about the same functionality as an Apple watch. And, for $99, you could buy one for a friend and still save money.
The only thing I see is that is not the end of the world. My FitBit would do a good job of tracking steps that maybe weren't actual steps - like when mountain biking, building trails, I always was over 10,000 steps. First day with this watch I figured out - it only tracks steps - so my numbers hover at 5,000 to 6,000 now for steps taken. This is more accurate but I do miss the big numbers!
Looking for an easy to use, full functional, smart watch - $99 gets you and awful lot. had I paid $199 I would still be writing the same review.
They did not pay me to write this. Today, after I had it charge from 8% to 100% in just over an hour, I thought the seller/manufacturer deserved the review.

I'm really enjoying this watch. I'm pleasantly surprised with the Zepo app. It has a lot of metrics that I've found useful. I recently had surgery, and it's been interesting to see how my sleep and activity were affected and to watch my scores begin to return to normal. Also, because I'm trying to eat more protein to help with healing, the app makes it easy to track my macros.
The battery life is great. It typically lasts about a week or 8 days, but if I track a lot of exercise, I do have to charge a day or two sooner.
I have a small wrist, and it doesn't overwhelm my wrist and look ridiculous, but it's large enough to be easy to use the screen.
I used to have a Tic watch, which they stopped making,but it stopped charging after a few years. I did look at other Google OS watches, but I couldn't find one that had as many features as the Amazfit Active 2 for about the same price. I also really prefer not to have to charge it as frequently. The ecosystem isn't quite as rich as the Google os, but I miss very little. And since I bought it during the Prime sale, I was pleased with the price.
The watch looks good, and there are a lot of alternative straps available (I wasn't a fan of the straps that came with the watch).
I compared heart rate, respiration, and oxygen saturation using a finger pulse-ox meter, and the watch matched up almost perfectly.
