This makes it hard to adjust posture as your clothes want to stay on the seat while you inevitably adjust your posture 100 times a minute because nothing is comfortable. I can't imagine what this is like in a slightly warm room.
Finally, the headrest - a bit too high at it's lowest setting (although I have a short waist so I won't blame the chair for this, even though a lot of people will be shorter than me who use this chair). Also, it is very unstable - every time you put your head back on it, it will move to a different position, and the hinge is far too loose so it wobbles like crazy. Kinda a nitpick and I could live with this but worth noting.
To summarize, the biggest issue is the shape of the seat, considering I'm an average sized human, it should not feel like I'm constantly falling off the chair. I have 3 roommates and each of them sat in the chair and were shocked at how it felt, before I even said much about it being uncomfortable. I'd genuinely rather sit on the floor than in this chair.

Bought this keyboard for my office, as a replacement for a wireless, membrane based keyboard that was starting to show its age.
The value of this keyboard is excellent.  Based on the feel, it seems to be a true mechanical keyboard with switches, and not a simulated one using a membrane contact with a clicky mechanism.  The feel is great and the pressure is just right to prevent most accidental touches to adjacent keys from inserting extra letters.  Nice and clicky, maybe not the best for noise if you're in an office with other people, but the feel is great and if you work in a private office like I do the noise won't matter much.  I had thought the RGB colors would be distracting, especially for an office, but actually they are fairly subdued and actually seem to help with positioning (I am a fast hunt-and-peck 3 finger typist, so this actually matters a lot to me).
I have a much more expensive Razer mechanical gaming keyboard at home, and the main difference I see between them, other than cosmetic differences, is that the Razer keys seem like they have a hair trigger and require very little motion to produce keystrokes, while this keyboard is a bit stiffer and requires the keys to be depressed a little harder in order to produce a keystroke.  So if you are relying on a hair trigger response for gaming, this maybe is not the best choice, although for a casual gamer like me it's more than adequate.  But for actually getting work done, the hair-trigger of the Razer keyboard makes it really hard not to make typos, and this keyboard is a lot better in that regard.
One minor nitpick is that the font used to label the keys is a little odd, and the "6" really, really looks like a "G", which can be a little off-putting at first.  But that's just a minor quibble.
Final verdict:  Definitely worth buying, unless you're an absolutely elite hardcore gamer.

The black color is a deep hue, & the chair has a stiff, heavy mesh fabric on its back & neck areas; 5, large legs with the moving ball feet at the bottoms of each leg, & a large chair cushion on which to sit which is soft but firm.  My approximate measurement sizes of parts of the chair are all according to my husband's adjustments to the chair in some places, & they are in no particular order as follows: Seat Cushion - 19"L x 19"W x 2 1/2" D; Back of Chair - 22" L x 19" W; Neck Rest - 6 3/4" H x 13" W; Chair Height - 45 1/2"; Chair Width - 22"; Length of Chair Legs (not including balls at ends) - 13 1/4" L; Arm Rests - 10"L x 4 1/4"W.  It is, overall, a solidly comfortable, roomy chair that supports our backs & bodies very well in general, plus it has specific lumbar, neck & arm supports.  It was not difficult for us to assemble, however either one of us could have done the same individually.  A few of the parts are rather heavy - the chair weighs about 40# - so it was great for one of us to hold a piece while the other secured it.  There are written directions included, however we both felt that easier to follow as well as informative instructions were on the item description area online, & the illustrative photos of the chair were helpful, too.  It took us less than 1 hour to assemble it.  The greatest thing to us is it is already proving to be helpful for my husband back when he sits in it - he loves the comfort & strong support for his entire body when he's sitting in the chair.  For reference, he is 6'1" tall, & he could easily adjust it - all over the chair - to his height as well as to his back areas where he needs extra support.  He says he likes the lumbar & neck supports the best.  This chair appears to be well made, with solid, weighty construction, with good hardware that fits the chair perfectly with no problems, with smooth rolling, ball feet, & with no creaking or listing of the chair after assembly.  I also feel it is a good value given its quality; its professional, sleek appearance; & its ability to be fully adjustable for one's body structure.  My husband & I both look forward to using this sturdy, comfy chair for many years of dependable, ergonomic support, & I highly recommend it!

I like this chair and find it comfortable to use, but there are a few areas where it could be improved.
Assembly took me about an hour, mostly because I had to reinstall the armrests after realizing I had attached them incorrectly. While the armrests were labeled left and right, the seat itself wasn't clearly marked front and back, so it wasn't immediately obvious how everything should be oriented, specially for someone assembling the office chair for the first time. The armrests installation allows for a small amount of wider or narrower positioning because of the oval mounting holes, which lets you fine-tune their width slightly. I also found that it was much easier to place the seat on the chair base first and then attach the backrest, even though the instructions suggest doing it in the opposite order. The headrest installation was also a bit confusing, and I had some difficulty getting the parts to align properly.
The chair itself is comfortable. The seat is wide, and the cushioning feels balanced - not too soft and not too firm. I used it for one-two hours, and it was pretty comfortable. The lumbar support is decent, and the headrest is a nice feature that I found quite useful.  I also like that the backrest reclines when you lean into it and automatically provides resistance, making it comfortable to sit back without having to adjust anything.
I also do like how adjustable the armrests are. However, the forward/backward and swivel adjustments move way too easy. When I'm trying to pull the chair by grabbing an armrest, the armrest changes position instead of staying where it was set. Those adjustments should have a firmer lock.
This is a comfortable, supportive office chair with a spacious seat, swlf-reclining backrest and good adjustment options for the armrests, armrest height, and headrest position. My main drawbacks were the assembly instructions, a few details in the installation process, and the armrest movement.

It's surprisingly hard to find neckband earbuds with ANC and even harder to find ones with decent battery life so I was really excited to find these for under $100.
Over the years I developed a habit of having earbuds in when I sleep, now I can't sleep without them. I've been through many sets of earbuds, I have a favorite until they inevitably get discontinued, and then I move on to the next thing.
Well, this is the next thing after my Soundcore earbuds got discontinued, and let me tell you, they're really... okay lol.
The price at $55 is higher than I usually go for, but the promise of ANC with multiple days of battery life convinced me to give it a try. The ANC is pretty good, the only thing I have to compare it to are the Status Between 3 ANC earbuds and it seems to be just as good as those.
Now for the elephant in the room, the sound quality. The biggest problem these have is when the low end comes in it overpowers the mids and highs and makes them sound muddy. Even if you're not an audiophile you'd probably notice the issue.
If you however adjust the EQ to bring down the lower frequencies, it's much much better. When the mids and highs aren't being drowned out, it's actually quite nice and there's still enough left in the low end to fill things out.
This could just be a bad factory EQ and not necessarily purely a limitation of the hardware, but that's Rythflo's problem to solve. Not everyone is going to want to download an EQ app just to make their $60 earbuds sound decent. Adjustments definitely need to be made.
So why 4 stars? Because overall they're fine and they check all the boxes for me and it does deliver on everything else. Neckband style, ANC, long battery life, okay to pretty decent audio quality depending if you want to adjust the EQ or not.

I've owned it for 4 days. I've made 10 full pots so far and three half carafe's.
1. Disregard the manual suggested scoops for a carafe. Unless you like strong thick bitter mud.
2. I suggest you use FP coarse if using quality coffee. If using grocery store ( like Tim Hortons preground)... I've dialed that in to 3 level large scoops for a full carafe ( obviously subjective). Any more than that gets progressively bitter and nasty.
I use #4 sun bleached paper filters.
Regarding the scoop. Well done Ninja. Conveniently attached to the coffee maker and well marked.
3. Expect a drop .... maybe two to drip on the burner when pulling the full carafe out. Sometimes it happens.Sometimes not. Small thing to me.
4. Do yourself a favor and search keywords, ' algae' and 'cleaning'. There is concern about the water retained in the bubble in the bottom of the water reservoir over time. Based on what I've read this is a common issue with multiple brands of coffee makers. I am going to make a point of leaving the lid open and  not queuing up coffee the night before, and emptying that bubble by pressing in the spring. Hoping that makes a difference. I will post and update the review occasionally.
5. I have measured  the brewing temperature of the water between 193 to 203.
6. There is a bloom. .
7. Classic vs. Rich: (edit) I've now had the Ninja for over a month. Until a week ago every pot or mug was made on 'classic'. Tried 'rich' a week ago. Much much better! A full taste. Not overly processed: not bitter, etc. THIS is the way. (Same coarse grind and quantity I listed above.) Very pleased with this coffee maker.
There was a comment about a plastic taste. I do admit there is a lot of plastic and when unboxing and assembling it was noticable. I followed instructions and ran 3 pots of water through it. The smell diminished but was not eliminated. As of day 4 after 10+ pots of coffee, I cannot smell plastic at all and I have never ( thankfully) tasted plastic in any brewed cup. Edit: now over a month.... plastic smell still completely gone.
Reliability seems to be a concern. I do realize that people with problems post more than those without. I elected to get the 4 year warranty ' just in case'. And I always have a French Press available for the inevitable day when it stops working ( hopefully at least 5 years from now).
I like this coffee maker. Makes excellent coffee. If it lasts, I'd buy another from Ninja.
Absolutely need to use a coarse grind to like the ratios suggested in the Ninja manual.

⭐️Original Review:
My husband and I are huge coffee lovers and have tried many types of brewers over the years. This Ninja was purchased in early August, and I intentionally waited until October to write my initial review so I could give a thorough, real-use perspective.
I can say with 100% confidence — this is the best coffee maker I’ve ever owned.
We are already a Ninja-product family, so I was excited to add this to our kitchen — but this machine completely exceeded expectations. I originally thought I was a simple “coffee + creamer” person, but this opened up a whole new world of drinks I didn’t even realize I’d enjoy.
My husband loves experimenting with flavors, foam, and different styles, and he is thrilled with how much versatility this one machine offers.
This coffee maker is used at least 4–5 times every single day (no judgment 😅), and every time we use it, we’re able to make something different — hot coffee, iced coffee, lattes, cappuccinos, and more.
☕ What You Get:
Coffee maker unit
Smart scoop (labeled per serving size)
Frother wand attachment
Tempered glass carafe with smart funnel
Permanent filter + filter basket
Flip-top water reservoir
De-clogger tool
Instruction manual
Usage & Features:
Cup Size Options:
Cup
XL Cup
Travel Tumbler
Multi-Serve Tumbler
Half Carafe
Full Carafe
You can switch between sizes easily with a simple knob turn.
Drip Stop Feature:
Acts like a quick pause, allowing you to pour a cup mid-brew without making a mess — super useful when brewing larger amounts.
Even when making a small cup, it still tastes like a full, properly brewed pot — not watered down like some machines. It takes a few minutes to fully extract flavor, which makes a noticeable difference.
☕ Brew Styles:
Classic
Rich
Over Ice
For iced coffee, I fill a cup with ice, add fresh coffee grounds to the filter, and brew using the “Over Ice” setting — it comes out perfectly balanced and not diluted.
Frother Wand:
One of my favorite features.
Add milk or creamer to a cup, place it under the wand, and run it for about 30 seconds — it creates a smooth foam that takes drinks to another level.
Cleaning & Storage:
Cleaning is simple and low maintenance:
Filters remove easily for rinsing
All removable parts are dishwasher safe
Grounds are easy to discard and clean out
When the descale light comes on, running a vinegar + water cycle through the reservoir gets everything back to normal quickly.
The adjustable platform is also great — it flips up to fit larger tumblers or the full carafe.
⚠️ Things to Know:
This machine does not use pods or K-cups
It is designed for ground coffee only
Personally, I actually prefer this — it’s much easier to clean a filter than deal with small reusable pods.

This quickly became my favorite appliance in the house, and I recommend it to anyone looking for a reliable, versatile coffee maker.

I never write reviews, but if you’re like me, you’re going to research new coffee machines like it’s your second job… hah. So here I am, about a month into owning the 10 cup model with an honest review. I LOVE IT. Between me and my husband, we use it 2-3x a day and have nothing but praise for it. We are not coffee snobs by any means, but we wanted to get away from kcups/nespresso pods (due to the waste) and after using a Keurig for many years, decided to make the switch to this very popular machine. I didn’t have too many requirements other than something programmable and the ability to brew different amounts.
I’ll start with the things I love about it:
1. Easy setup + use. After everything was washed and I ran a clean cycle, the machine was ready for use. To brew coffee, you select the size then choose if you want “classic” or “rich”. Once you select, it starts blinking and then will begin to brew shortly after. Brew times are fairly quick, no complaints there. A full carafe (on the classic setting) brews in roughly 8 minutes. The delay brew option is easy to use as well. I usually set up the machine at night for my husband so he has coffee waiting for him at 5:30a when he gets up for work. The machine brews in a few minutes and is fairly quiet — it does beep several times once done, but does not disturb me or our young toddler. I don’t find it loud or disruptive.
2. Features. Honestly, this machine is well equipped for under $200. Several options for brew sizes, the classic vs rich, option to brew a specialty 4oz cup (not espresso since it doesn’t get hot enough, but I’m not picky and it works for a quick at home option), brew over ice, and of course the built in frother. It would be nice if the frother warmed the milk too, but I just pop it into the microwave to heat prior to frothing. Froths nicely! I also really love the included measuring scoop. It attaches to the machine for convenience. I follow the guides for number of scoops and use it every time I need to measure the grounds.
3. The aesthetic look of the machine and feel of quality. It looks nice on my kitchen counter and doesn’t take up a lot of room. Plus it’s nice the frother folds in to make it even more compact. The included glass carafe feels good and doesn’t feel cheap or too thin. Overall I feel the quality of the machine is nice for the price.
I read a lot of the complaints, which I’ve had zero issues with. There is no plastic taste/smell anywhere on the machine. I did thoroughly wash each piece and ran a clean cycle prior to use, but I didn’t even notice a smell when I unpacked the machine. Coffee is plenty hot and there is even a “stay warm” feature you can choose after brewing your coffee (it does automatically come on after brewing a half/full carafe), but sometimes I will use the multi serve option and brew it into the included carafe then turn on the stay warm feature if it’s going to take me more than a bit to drink the 2 cups I usually get from it. I wrote a full review for this item before the Amazon app glitched and I lost a full page of notes.  I'm not going to go through that trouble again, but you NEED to know one thing before purchasing:
Whatever this thing can do, something else can do better.  The only "up" this has on other wearables is the battery life--which is great.
Everything else is outperformed by competitors.  I had a Samsung Watch 5 Pro that could tell me what exercise I was doing (lifting weights, walking, napping, etc.) at all times.  This Whoop asks you what exercise you were doing, and if it's not on the list then you can't enter it on your own.  Taking a shower?  This device will think you were swimming.
Blood pressure monitoring?  It's a fake.  If you go to the trouble of using an actual cuff and enter manual readings, the Whoop can give you a good estimate.  That estimate is based on analyzing your activity and other metrics, though, not on actually measuring your bp.  Blood sugar was teased as a possible function in the future.  There's no way this thing could do this accurately in this version.
Accessories like new bands have to be purchased in the Whoop store.  I had to spend $50.00 for a brown fabric band because nothing was available from retailers.  Want a custom band or something nicer?  You're gonna have to pay big.
Battery life is great.  You'll get 14 to 16 days every time.  That was an important consideration when making this purchase and it's the only thing that has impressed me.
The app and the user interface is clunky and uncompromising.  There's no way to customize the display or rearrange widgets that I have been able to find.
I bought this item to replace a Samsung Watch 5 Pro because I needed something with better battery life.  I got it.  Absolutely nothing else is better after three months (plus) with the Whoop.
Save your money and spend it on something better.

I purchased WHOOP hoping for deep insights into my health, recovery, sleep, fitness, and overall wellness. After spending considerable time with it, I have mixed feelings.
The biggest issue is the subscription cost. The hardware is only part of the expense, and the ongoing membership adds up quickly. For that price, I expected more detailed analysis and actionable information than what I ultimately received.
WHOOP does provide a lot of data, but much of it feels surface-level. You'll get recovery scores, strain scores, sleep metrics, HRV, resting heart rate, biological age estimates, and other wellness indicators. The app does a good job explaining what the numbers mean, but often the insights feel simplified rather than truly in-depth.
The platform seems heavily focused on recovery metrics, biological age, and overall wellness trends rather than providing detailed explanations of what's actually driving the results. After a while, it can feel like you're repeatedly looking at scores and summaries without gaining significantly deeper understanding.
I also found the device somewhat "judgmental" in how it handles wear time. If you remove it briefly for something as simple as a shower, it can impact tracking and make it feel like you're being penalized for not wearing it continuously.
Some features were more impressive than others. The ECG capability is interesting, but it's not automatically monitoring—you have to actively perform the measurement. The blood pressure estimates appear to rely heavily on calibration and prior measurements rather than direct continuous readings.
Accuracy was mixed. Heart rate tracking generally seemed reasonable, but I found oxygen saturation readings often differed from dedicated fingertip pulse oximeters I own. That made me question how much confidence I should place in some of the health metrics.
The battery life is good, the device is comfortable, and the app is easy to use. However, for the monthly cost, I expected deeper analytics, more medical-grade accuracy, and more meaningful insights beyond the recovery and biological age focus.
If you're highly interested in recovery tracking and wellness trends, WHOOP may be a good fit. If you're looking for detailed health analytics and comprehensive fitness data, make sure you understand exactly what you're paying for before committing to the subscription.

I've been using the AirPods 4 for a little while now, and after spending enough time with them during work, walks, and random YouTube binges, I think they're a solid upgrade—but not a perfect one.
Coming from the AirPods 3, the first thing I noticed was the fit. These are definitely more comfortable in my ears. I can wear them much longer without constantly adjusting them or feeling like one is about to make a dramatic leap onto the sidewalk. If you've ever done the awkward "catch the falling earbud" dance in public, you know exactly what I mean.
The sound quality is better than the AirPods 3, but honestly, don't expect your favorite songs to suddenly sound like you're sitting front row at a live concert. The improvements are there—music sounds a little fuller, vocals are cleaner, and overall audio has a bit more depth—but it's more of a "nice, I can hear the difference" upgrade rather than a "wow, my life has changed" moment.
One feature I absolutely love is the ear detection. It's almost creepy how well it works. I take one earbud out, and the music pauses instantly. Put it back in, and it picks up right where I left off without me touching anything. It's one of those small features you don't think about until it works so well that you forget it's even happening.
Now for my biggest complaint: the battery life. This was honestly the most disappointing part for me. I expected at least the same endurance as my AirPods 3, but these seem to need charging sooner. They're far from terrible, but I definitely find myself putting them back in the case more often than I expected. It's not a dealbreaker, but it's enough that I noticed it pretty quickly.
Setup was exactly what you'd expect with Apple—open the case near my iPhone, tap connect, and that's basically it. No headaches, no digging through Bluetooth settings, and no wondering if I accidentally paired them with my neighbor's phone instead.
Overall, I'm giving these 4 stars because I genuinely enjoy using them every day. They're more comfortable, sound a little better, and all the little Apple conveniences just work the way they're supposed to. I just wish Apple had squeezed in a little more battery life because that would've made these an easy five-star product.
What I Like
The fit is noticeably more comfortable than my AirPods 3 and stays secure in my ears.
The sound quality is better with clearer vocals and fuller audio.
The ear detection works flawlessly every single time.
Setup with my iPhone took less than a minute.
The USB-C charging case is a welcome upgrade since I can finally stop carrying another cable.
What I Don't Like
The battery life feels shorter than I expected and is my biggest complaint.
The sound improvement is noticeable but not dramatic if you're already using AirPods 3.
Summary
If you're using older AirPods or just want a more comfortable pair that works effortlessly with your iPhone, the AirPods 4 are definitely worth buying. The better fit, reliable features, and improved sound make everyday listening enjoyable, even if the battery life isn't quite as impressive as I hoped. They're not a revolutionary upgrade, but they're a really good one—and aside from wishing they could stay alive a little longer between charges, I've been happy reaching for them every day.

This review provides a list of my observations about the 21.4 inch (call it 22) Philips VA monitor 221V8LB.  (Note: monitor sizes are measured *diagonally*, width and height are smaller.)  But first let me explain why I got this monitor to replace my almost ten year old 27 inch HP IPS monitor 27wm.  While the HP monitor was still fine, it had some superficial surface damage, visible under certain light, that annoyed me.  And I decided I really wanted a smaller monitor to replace it.  Cataract surgery, combined with one particularly problematic eye, has left me unable to focus at different distances.  And progressive glasses are fine for driving a car or other vehicle, but not for much else.  So I wear my reading glasses to view my monitor.  And if the center of my 27 inch monitor was in maximum focus at about 12 inch, the corners really started getting far enough to get a bit fuzzy.  In addition my eyes are very long, reducing my peripheral vision, so having the corners at a very large angle was awkward.  A smaller size monitor, but of the same full HD resolution, like my laptop, seemed a good idea.  And 22 inch seemed to be about the smallest they sell nowadays.  (Also, while my laptop screen is a lot smaller at 13.25 inch, when I am traveling I do find that really too small to see easily.)  The Philips was cheap, and worked out well in increasing my comfort.  The list of my observations now follows.
1) Power cable.  The monitor comes with a relatively short power cable of about 5 ft; too short for me to pull the monitor towards me when I am sitting back in my chair.  For comparison, the HP power cord was a bit over 6 ft.  In addition, you cannot simply switch power cords, because the Philips comes with a highly unusual monitor power connector.  So, if 5 ft is too short, you may need some sort of extension cord.  I had one handy, but if you do not, factor in another $5 or whatever and the hassle of getting one.  (I do not know how many people return the monitor because the cord is not long enough, but I suspect the manufacturer might be penny-wise and dollar-foolish.)  (I initially measured the length as 54 inch and was planning to subtract a star, but 5 ft vs 6 ft seems a bit too small for that, though the nonstandard cable does not help.)
2) Speakers.  There are no speakers in this model, and the web page never claims there are.  (But it also does not highlight that they are missing.  Not smart, if you ask me.  Think of all the hassle and expense of the user returning the product.)  Apparently you need a model name ending in an A (for audio?) to get speakers.  However, there *is* an aux port, unlike one review said.  I found this aux port *very* convenient, as for unknown reasons the aux port on my docking station stopped working a long time ago.  Now I could connect my aux stereo speakers plus woofer permanently to my monitor instead of awkwardly to my laptop itself.  (Actually, I could do this also with my old monitor, but I never thought of it at all, and would have needed a HDMI cable instead of my VGA one.  VGA does not do audio.)  Note that analog aux is not going to be of the quality that digital HDMI could in principle provide.  One reviewer complained that aux speakers are almost impossible to get nowadays.  Well, as I write this, go to a big cheap department store near you and there they are for $13.  I got these earlier for my spare old laptop and they work fine.
3) HDMI cable.  The reviews AI claimed that some users complained of not getting a HDMI cable.  Well, I went over the most recent reviews as of Oct 14, 2025, and I found 9 reviews explicitly stating that the HDMI cable was there and only 3 saying it was not.  I suspect that these 3 may have bought used "like new" monitors, though only one of the 3 said so explicitly.  Unlike the power cord, the HDMI cable turned out to be long enough for me to duct it through the cable guide of my MOUNTUP stand.  It is hard for me to measure it accurately in its convoluted path, but it seems to be about 55 inch.

The panel offers the smoothest video you can find in this price range monitor. Colors are very nice and close to real (needs some tuning and adjustment). Colors are very alive and deep right out of the box; with some tuning, you can adjust it very close to what you see every day on your iPhone (iPhone user here, eyes are trained for that screen).
Brightness was another winning point. Comparing to the other 3 panels that I tried, this panel offers the best lighting. With other panels, what I noticed was that they get either too bright or too dim. This would really bother me playing battle royale games, constantly changing zones from dark to bright. Regardless of the adjustments, my screen would be either too bright that it would hurt eyes, or too dim, which would bother you and distract you from gameplay to mess with monitor brightness settings. However, this panel does not have any of those issues. It offers very balanced lighting regardless of how quickly the lighting changes from dark to bright.
Performance-wise, this monitor shows picture in fast-action games with 0 blurring. I own an RTX 4070, and Apex Legends is my benchmark for performance since I have played this game for a long time. I benchmark hardware in this game because I am used to all the values and metrics in this game. Regardless of how fast you turn and move the screen, you will not see any blurring or delay for pixels refreshing. 280 strong hertz are packed in this panel.
The other reason I chose this monitor was its OLED care system. I heard that due to its newer technology it has a lower risk of getting OLED burn issues; however, it does the OLED care job very well by itself. Every time you shut down the PC, the monitor goes into a screen cleaning mode to maintain the pixels. Every time you turn on the PC, the monitor shows you a message that OLED screen cleaning happened and it was successful, so no need for manually going through settings and activating OLED screen care like ASUS monitors.
It has an RGB light in the back, which I do not really care for. It is very basic and simple, does not have any special effects or anything—just breathe, rainbow, and a few solid colors. The only good thing I like about the RGB is that it signals you when the monitor is doing its OLED self-care screen cleaning by doing a rainbow animation thing.
So far, durable. Been using it for a few months now, and without doing any manual screen cleaning, I do not have any screen burn. I have Wallpaper Engine on my PC, so I have animated wallpapers that always change + my taskbar goes hidden.
The panel is surprisingly thin and lightweight. Coming from a curved monitor, I was not expecting the panel to be this thin and this lightweight! I had to readjust the spring on my monitor arm; if not, it would shoot the monitor into the ceiling lol!
I did not upload any pictures, because what you see on your device is never the same as what you will see on the actual screen.

This is a true next step in OLED monitors with the Tandem OLED panel. This monitor looks just as good as previous model OLEDs but I am very happy that it now gets much brighter while also having less of a risk of burn in compared to previous generations of OLED monitors. The monitor itself was very easy to set up and came with all the cables I needed.
The first main thing I like about this monitor, honestly, is the stand itself. The stand is not only very sturdy and helps to keep it firmly on my desk, but the monitor can adjust way better than any other monitor I've owned. In the past, it would be a struggle for me to raise the monitor to a comfortable eye level for me as most sit too low, but this one is perfect for me. It also swivels left and right and the screen itself can be rotated. So, regardless of what your use case for this monitor is, you definitely don't need another stand as the one it comes with is more than capable.
As far as the quality of the monitor itself goes, I was blown away. I had been using a 4K display, so I was worried that the lower 2K resolution would be very noticeable. Fortunately, the downgrade in resolution was not nearly as noticeable as I thought it would be and the screen remains sharp and clear. Online videos, games, and general use all look great. The only issue I noticed is that the text fringing on some OLEDs is still semi apparent, but after my first couple of hours it was a non-issue for me.  The screen was very easy to adjust to my preferred settings, but the display was very vibrant out of the box. I personally prefer brighter displays as sometimes even a very color accurate display would still look dull to me without the brightness to make it "pop." Previous OLEDs were borderline too dull for me, and I also knew that increasing the brightness would increase the burn in risk. With this new Tandem OLED model, I am happy to say that it gets almost nearly as bright as my main 4K Mini-LED display. The refresh rate is also easy on the eyes, and the fast response times make it feel snappy.
The only main downside I've noticed about this display is that HDR content in Windows still leaves something to be desired. I mainly use the display in SDR as it is brighter on average for me and I don't have to mess around with the HDR settings constantly. Maybe it's just me never really liking the HDR implementation on Windows, but it is worth noting. Some games also have VRR flicker, but it is barely noticeable to my eyes and only sometimes shows up in darker scenes.
My overall high score for this monitor, however, is due to the value. Previous OLEDs I've tried in the past were far more costly yet had duller screens, higher burn in risk, and questionable warranty at times. With this model, the new Tandem OLED panel really does bridge the gap in terms of brightness, while also giving more vibrant colors. This feels like the first true example of what an OLED monitor should be, and I can't wait to see where future models go from here on out. I highly recommend it.
